quote: a 16-bit chip whose instruction set no descendant has ever removed
problem: This is literally false twice over. The 8086's POP CS (opcode 0F) was dropped from the 80186/80286 onward, and its byte was reused as the two-byte opcode escape. x86-64's 64-bit mode makes AAA, DAA, PUSH/POP of segment registers and other 8086 instructions invalid. It also turns the 8086's one-byte INC/DEC opcodes 40 to 4F into REX prefixes: the 48 that opens Fig 3.1 was DEC AX on the 8086. What is true is that every x86-64 chip can still run 8086 code in its legacy modes. Sources: felixcloutier.com/x86/aaa ("Invalid" in 64-bit mode); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64 (decimal arithmetic and segment push/pop not supported in 64-bit mode).
fix: "In 1978, Intel released the 8086, a 16-bit chip whose programs every descendant can still run." The next sentence stays.
reason: 'No descendant has ever removed' is literally false. POP CS (0F) was dropped from the 80186/286 and its byte became the two-byte escape. In 64-bit mode AAA, DAA, PUSH/POP of segment registers and others are invalid, and 8086's one-byte INC/DEC 40-4F became REX prefixes (Fig 3.1's own 48 was DEC AX on the 8086). It is the chapter's opening sentence and a fact claim the §4g law covers. The next sentence already says 'core binary patterns', so the repair is to make the first sentence match.
judge_fix: "In 1978, Intel released the 8086, a 16-bit chip whose instruction set its descendants have extended but never replaced." The next sentence stays. Sources: felixcloutier.com/x86/aaa ('Invalid' in 64-bit mode); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86-64.
